acts: Andhra Pradesh Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986
records.person: A man from Panyam; his wife brought the petition
records.summary: Nandyal's district collector ordered a man detained without trial as a 'bootlegger' because of four cases against him under the prohibition law, in every one of which courts had already granted him bail. The state confirmed the detention in September 2025. On 5 May 2026 the High Court set the order aside and directed his release.
detail: On 24 July 2025 the Collector and District Magistrate of Nandyal ordered the preventive detention of the petitioner's husband, treating him as a 'bootlegger' under section 2(b) of the 1986 preventive-detention law. The High Court recorded that 'about four crimes were registered against the detenu for the offences punishable under the A.P. Prohibition Act' and that 'conditional bail was granted to him in all the said four crimes'.

The detaining authority reasoned that his repeated offences were 'prejudicial to the maintenance of public order and posing danger to public safety and health'. The State confirmed the order by G.O.Rt. No. 1614 on 3 September 2025, 'and since then he has been in custody', the court recorded.

A Division Bench of Justices Cheekati Manavendranath Roy and Tuhin Kumar Gedela held that the bail orders, and the effect of their conditions, had not been placed before and weighed by the detaining authority, which 'invalidates the order of preventive detention'. It set the order aside and directed that he 'be released forthwith'.
The judgment records no allegation of violence, of spurious or poisonous liquor, or of harm to any person. The only conduct it mentions is repeated offences under the prohibition law.
records.current_position: Detention set aside on 5 May 2026 and release ordered. The four Prohibition Act cases themselves are not described in the judgment.

records.title: Rs 2 lakh food-safety fine in a tobacco case set aside nine years later
records.authority: Joint Collector-cum-Adjudicating Officer, Guntur (penalty); High Court of Andhra Pradesh (set aside)
records.case_reference: Crl.R.C. No. 210 of 2019; Crl.A. No. 100 of 2018 (Principal District and Sessions Judge, Guntur); Rc. No. 1024/2017-L.2
laws: Section 96, Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006
records.person: A resident of Macherla
records.penalty: Rs 2,00,000, reduced to Rs 70,000 on appeal; both set aside
records.summary: In November 2017 Guntur's joint collector fined a Macherla man Rs 2 lakh under the food-safety law; on appeal the fine was cut to Rs 70,000. On 6 August 2026 the High Court set both orders aside, applying its settled view that chewing tobacco and khaini are not 'food', so the food-safety law cannot be used to punish trade in them.
detail: The High Court recorded that on 16 November 2017 the Joint Collector-cum-Adjudicating Officer, Guntur, imposed a penalty of Rs 2,00,000 on the petitioner under section 96 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. On appeal, the Principal District and Sessions Judge, Guntur, reduced it to Rs 70,000 on 30 January 2019.

The petitioner's counsel relied on earlier High Court rulings that chewing tobacco and khaini are not food within the Act, and that trade in tobacco is governed by the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act, 2003, not the food-safety law. One of those rulings, quoted in the order, notes that 'the trade in Tobacco is not impermissible in India'.

Justice Y. Lakshmana Rao held that, 'in view of the constant view taken by this Court', the Sessions judgment and the collector's order were 'liable to be interfered and set aside', and set both aside on 6 August 2026.
records.current_position: Penalty set aside on 6 August 2026, nearly nine years after it was imposed.

records.title: Police charged a Visakhapatnam shopkeeper with 'poisoning' for storing e-cigarettes; High Court quashes the case
records.authority: Visakhapatnam City police (prosecution); High Court of Andhra Pradesh (quashed)
records.case_reference: Crl.P. No. 12896 of 2025; C.C. No. 2896 of 2025 (IV Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Visakhapatnam); FIR No. 57 of 2024, III Town Police Station
laws: Section 5 read with section 8, Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019
Sections 284 and 328, Indian Penal Code, 1860
records.person: A shopkeeper in Visakhapatnam
records.summary: In March 2024 Visakhapatnam's City Task Force raided shops selling e-cigarettes and charged a shopkeeper not only under the e-cigarette ban but under penal-code sections for negligence with poison and for causing hurt by poison. On 9 March 2026 the High Court quashed the whole prosecution: e-cigarettes are not 'poison', and the storage offence is non-cognizable, so police could not file a charge sheet for it.
detail: The Hindu reported on 24 March 2024 that Visakhapatnam's City Task Force raided two shops, arrested two people for selling banned e-cigarettes, and seized several hundred of them.

III Town police registered FIR No. 57 of 2024 under section 5 read with section 8 of the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019, which bans storing e-cigarettes, and under sections 284 and 328 of the Indian Penal Code, which punish negligent conduct with poisonous substances and causing hurt by poison. A charge sheet followed, and the case was numbered C.C. No. 2896 of 2025.

Justice Y. Lakshmana Rao held that e-cigarettes are not a 'poisonous substance' under section 284, and that the facts alleged did not amount to administering poison under section 328. He further held that the storage offence under the e-cigarette law is non-cognizable, so it had to be pursued by a written complaint from an authorised officer, not a police charge sheet. The proceedings were quashed.
records.current_position: Prosecution quashed by the High Court on 9 March 2026.

quote.heading: What the High Court held
quote.text: Electronic cigarettes, which form the subject matter of the present prosecution, do not, by any legally tenable construction or judicial interpretation, answer the description of a 'poisonous substance' within the contemplation of Section 284 of 'the I.P.C.,' nor do the facts alleged constitute the administration of poison or stupefying substances as envisaged under Section 328 of 'the I.P.C.'
quote.where: Crl.P. No. 12896 of 2025, judgment dated 9 March 2026, para 6

sections.text: Adults who buy e-cigarettes choose to. The shopkeeper was prosecuted for keeping them in stock, and police added poisoning charges that the High Court found had no legal basis.

records.title: Woman on hunger strike to meet the Chief Minister booked for attempted suicide
records.authority: Kakinada Urban police, on a complaint by the Mandal Executive Magistrate; recorded by the High Court of Andhra Pradesh
records.case_reference: Cr. No. 80 of 2023 (section 309 read with 34 IPC); W.P. No. 21912 of 2023 (High Court)
laws: Section 309 read with section 34, Indian Penal Code, 1860
records.person: A woman from Kakinada
records.summary: A Kakinada woman in a property dispute with two police constables went on hunger strike after being refused a meeting with the Chief Minister. According to the State, she was taken to hospital when her health deteriorated, tried to take her own life there, and was then booked for attempted suicide on the complaint of the local executive magistrate. On 6 January 2026 the High Court directed police not to interfere with her liberty except by due process.
detail: The woman petitioned the High Court alleging that police officers were harassing her and her disabled daughter and pressing her to settle a property dispute with two police constables on their terms, including by admitting the two of them to a mental hospital in Visakhapatnam.

The Assistant Government Pleader, on instructions, told the court that the Chief Minister's security staff did not allow her to meet the Chief Minister at his camp office; that when she sat on hunger strike a medical team advised shifting her to the Government Hospital as her health was deteriorating; and that she 'tried to commit suicide' after admission. On the complaint of the Mandal Executive Magistrate, Kakinada Urban, a case was registered under section 309 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, the offence of attempting suicide.

Justice Venkata Jyothirmai Pratapa disposed of the petition by directing the respondents 'not to interfere with the personal liberty of the petitioner and her daughter, except under due process of law'. The order does not deal with the attempted-suicide case itself.

Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 provides that a person who attempts suicide is presumed, unless proved otherwise, to have severe stress, and shall not be tried and punished under section 309.
records.current_position: The attempted-suicide case (Cr. No. 80 of 2023) was registered; its present status is not stated in the High Court order.

records.summary: Police in Bilaspur district prosecuted a man under Sections 294, 504 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code over a 2005 public incident, alleging he abused and threatened a local woman and behaved indecently in public while collecting water charges. detail: The High Court recorded that the police filed a challan under Sections 294, 504 and 506 IPC over an incident on 11 September 2005 at village Jaroda in Bilaspur district, during collection of water charges, alleging that the accused abused and threatened the informant and 'removed his pants and undergarments and started behaving indecently' in the presence of villagers.

The Judicial Magistrate First Class, Court No. 2, Ghumarwin (Bilaspur), acquitted the accused on 27 April 2010, citing unexplained delay in the FIR, failure of witnesses to state the exact act, examination of only inimical witnesses, and material contradictions. The State appealed to the High Court.

In Criminal Appeal No. 306 of 2010 decided on 27 May 2025, Justice Rakesh Kainthla dismissed the State's appeal. The court held that to prove an offence under Section 294 IPC it is not enough to utter or do something obscene: it must be proved to be to the annoyance of others, and no witness stated that he or she was annoyed.

The court also held the ingredients of Sections 504 and 506 IPC unproved (no intentional insult likely to provoke a breach of the peace, and no alarm caused), that the delay in lodging the FIR beyond 24 hours was unexplained, and that the trial court had taken a reasonable view. The acquittal was upheld.

Police cited Sections 296 and 79 of the BNS, Section 4 of the Indecent Representation of Women Act, Section 4 of the tobacco Act and Karnataka Police Act licensing provisions.

The High Court held that Section 296 requires an obscene act in or near a public place to cause annoyance to others; without evidence of actual annoyance to a third party, the obscenity claim could not continue.

The High Court noted there was no material to show that a statement from any woman against whom a Section 79 offence was alleged had been recorded under Section 183(6) BNSS. records.summary: Excise officials verbally ordered a licensed IMFL retailer to shut after church and committee complaints. The retailer said she was never heard before the closure. The High Court recorded that after operating briefly the retailer was verbally told by the Superintendent of Excise to shut following complaints from pastors of two churches, that she complied and remained shut, and that she was never afforded any opportunity to present her case before the closure.

The High Court recorded that an interim order dated 16.12.2025 directed verification of distances from churches and institutions and a meeting between the Deputy Commissioner, the retailer and the village headman, and that later minutes noted the outlet was about 200 metres from the churches with the required NOC obtained and no breach of Excise law.

Police said nothing in this matter about any victim: a news report of the ruling stated that moral objection by church elders and locals cannot be a ground to shut a licensed shop found beyond the mandatory 200-metre distance from places of worship.

records.title: Uttarakhand High Court sets aside an attempted-suicide conviction, invoking the Mental Healthcare Act
records.summary: The High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital allowed a criminal revision and set aside the judicial magistrate's 2023 conviction, later affirmed on appeal, of a Nagar Palika Parishad clerk from Manglaur (Haridwar district) under Section 309 IPC for allegedly attempting suicide in 2011. The single bench of Justice Pankaj Purohit held that the prosecution had not proved an attempt beyond the stage of preparation, and that Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 presumptively protects a person who attempts suicide from being tried or punished. The nominal sentence and fine were quashed.
records.authority: High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital
records.case_reference: Criminal Revision No.946 of 2024; Case Crime No.71 of 2011 (Kotwali Mangalore); Criminal Case No.873 of 2012 (New Criminal Case No.1114 of 2023), Judicial Magistrate Ist, Roorkee; Criminal Appeal No.34 of 2023
laws: Section 309 IPC
Section 115, Mental Healthcare Act, 2017
records.person: a clerk in the Nagar Palika Parishad office in Manglaur, Haridwar district
records.penalty: conviction and sentence (imprisonment till rising of the Court and a Rs 500 fine, with five days' simple imprisonment in default) set aside
detail: The High Court recorded that the revisionist was a clerk in the Nagar Palika Parishad, Manglaur, and that on 21.02.2011 constables posted at Kotwali Mangalore found him on the upper floor of the parishad building having poured kerosene upon himself and holding a matchbox; a plastic bottle of kerosene and a matchbox were recovered and Case Crime No.71 of 2011 under Section 309 IPC was registered. A medical examination the same day showed no external injury or kerosene poisoning, though the doctor noted the smell of kerosene on his head and upper body.

The Court noted that the Judicial Magistrate, Ist, Roorkee, convicted him on 11.07.2023 and sentenced him to imprisonment till rising of the Court with a fine of Rs 500 (five days' simple imprisonment in default), and that the Ist Additional Sessions Judge, Roorkee, dismissed Criminal Appeal No.34 of 2023 on 10.12.2024, affirming the conviction and sentence.

The Court held that no overt act towards self-destruction was committed and that the medical report and the evidence of the official witnesses did not show that the act had crossed the stage of preparation into attempt; the only independent witness did not support the prosecution. It found the essential ingredient of Section 309 IPC not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

The Court further held that the trial and appellate courts had proceeded 'in a routine and mechanical manner' and had failed to consider Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, which presumes severe stress and provides that such a person 'shall not be tried or punished' under Section 309 IPC; there was nothing on record to rebut that presumption.

The Court observed that the sentence was nominal but the stigma of conviction had badly affected the revisionist's government employment and mental health, and that the criminal justice system must not add to the suffering of those already under mental distress.
records.current_position: The criminal revision was allowed and the orders of 11.07.2023 and 10.12.2024 were set aside, so the conviction and sentence no longer stand.

The judgment does not record a district 'victim' because there was none. The incident date (21.02.2011) is from the judgment; the latest official act is the High Court order of 06.11.2025. Searches for a more recent (2026) Uttarakhand case of the same type - Indian Kanoon queries 'Uttarakhand "309 IPC" fromdate: 1-1-2026', 'Uttarakhand "attempt to suicide" fromdate: 1-1-2026', 'Uttarakhand suicide "BNS" fromdate: 1-1-2026', 'Uttarakhand "Mental Healthcare Act" fromdate: 1-1-2026', 'Uttarakhand Beggary fromdate: 1-1-2025', 'Uttarakhand beggar fromdate: 1-1-2025' and 'Uttarakhand obscenity fromdate: 1-1-2026' - found none that is victimless. records.title: Supreme Court quashed obscenity proceedings over nude sports photograph published in a Kolkata newspaper
records.summary: A private complainant initiated proceedings after an Indian sports magazine and a Kolkata newspaper published a nude photograph of an international tennis player and his fiancée. An Alipore magistrate found a prima facie case under Section 292 IPC and subsequently ordered the accused to face trial under that provision or, alternatively, Section 4 of the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986. The Supreme Court set aside the criminal proceedings after finding that the photograph and article were not obscene when viewed in context under the contemporary community-standards test.
records.authority: Supreme Court of India (prosecution by State of West Bengal)
records.case_reference: Supreme Court Criminal Appeal No. 902 of 2004, arising from Criminal Revision No. 1591 of 1994 before the Calcutta High Court

detail: The Supreme Court recorded that Sports World reproduced the article and photograph as its cover story on 05.05.1993 and that Anandabazar Patrika, a newspaper widely circulated in Kolkata, published them on 06.05.1993.
The Court recorded the magistrate's finding that 'a prima facie case is made out against the accused persons under Section 292 IPC.'

The Court applied the contemporary community-standards test and found that the photograph and article, viewed in the context of their anti-racism message, were not objectionable under Section 292 IPC or Section 4 of the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986.
The Court concluded: 'We are, therefore, inclined to allow this appeal and set aside the criminal proceedings initiated against the Appellants.'
records.current_position: Criminal proceedings were finally set aside by the Supreme Court.

records.title: High Court upholds acquittal in liquor-transport case after 19 years
records.summary: Police in Kangra district prosecuted a jeep driver for carrying 58 boxes of country liquor and five boxes of beer; a Jawali magistrate convicted him in 2007 and an appellate court acquitted him in 2013. On 24 September 2026 the Himachal Pradesh High Court dismissed the State's appeal, holding the sample evidence could not prove the contents were liquor.
records.date_label: High Court judgment dismissing State appeal
records.authority: Himachal Pradesh High Court, Justice Rakesh Kainthla
laws: Section 61(1)(a) of the Punjab Excise Act, 1914 (as applied in Himachal Pradesh)
records.person: a jeep driver in Kangra district
detail: The High Court recorded that police found 58 boxes of country liquor, each with 12 pouches of 750 ml, and 5 boxes of beer in a Mahindra jeep.
The Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate, Jawali convicted the driver on 01.02.2007; the Additional Sessions Judge, Kangra at Dharamshala acquitted him on 04.06.2013 and the State appealed.
The High Court held the chain of sampling was not proved, so the analysis report could not establish that the bottles and pouches held liquor, and that the appellate court's view was reasonable.
The High Court dismissed the appeal on 24 September 2026.
records.current_position: Acquittal upheld on 24 September 2026, 19 years after the trial-court conviction.
records.caveats: The trial record of 2007 was not read; the facts are as recorded in the High Court judgment.

quote.text: In view of the above, the present appeal fails, and it is dismissed.

records.title: High Court quashes 16-year-old immoral traffic case against a hotel customer
records.summary: Ahmedabad police raided a hotel in 2010 using a decoy customer and booked a man found there as a customer under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act. The Gujarat High Court quashed the FIR against him on 18 September 2026, sixteen years later.
records.date_label: High Court judgment quashing the FIR

records.case_reference: R/Criminal Misc. Application No. 7082 of 2018
laws: Sections 3, 5, 7 and 9 of the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956
Section 188 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
records.person: a man found at a hotel during a raid
detail: The High Court recorded that the FIR of 17.01.2010 at DCB Police Station said a hotel was running a brothel, and that police sent a decoy customer before raiding it.
The petitioner was shown by the investigating agency as a customer at the time of the raid, and argued the Act's sections could not be invoked against a customer.
The High Court quashed the FIR and all consequential proceedings against him.
records.current_position: Proceedings against the customer stand quashed.
records.caveats: The case against the hotel's operators is not covered by this order.
